I have been farming this 7.5 mu of land in Quzhou for 30 years, and I know every corner of it. My family has 8 mouths to feed, and with some of them working off-farm, we have a bit of cash to buy good inputs, but I still must be careful with every yuan. This year, I will keep my wheat-maize rotation because it is what this soil knows best.

I will plant winter wheat on all 7.5 mu as soon as the autumn rains soften the ground. I buy improved wheat seeds from the county supply store—yes, they cost more than saving my own grain, but they resist disease better and give fuller ears. Before sowing, I will rotary till the field to break up the stubble and make a fine seedbed. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as a base when I sow, and then top-dress with urea at the green-up and jointing stages in spring. My well gives me water when I need it, so I will irrigate three times: once after sowing to help emergence, once at jointing when the wheat is thirsty, and once during grain filling to plump the kernels. I will keep my eyes open for aphids and powdery mildew, and if I see them, I will spray twice—no more, because chemicals cost money and I don't want to poison the soil.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will waste no time. The very same day or the next, I will sow summer maize using hybrid seeds. There is no time to plough again, and the soil still holds moisture from the wheat field, so I will use no-tillage sowing. I will put down fertilizer with the seeder, and then sidedress more nitrogen when the maize reaches the big trumpet stage. I will irrigate twice—once when the tassels emerge and once during grain filling if the summer drought bites. I will watch for armyworms and corn borers, and spray twice if they appear. I expect my wheat to give me about 450 kg per mu and my maize about 550 kg per mu. That is enough to feed my household and sell a little to pay for next year's inputs and my grandchildren's school needs.
